claim: Sox21a is a group B Sox protein.
source: Sox21a, a group B Sox protein, is preferentially expressed in the committed progenitor named enteroblast (EB) to promote enterocyte differentiation.
evidence: Stated directly in the abstract

claim: Sox21a is preferentially expressed in enteroblasts (EBs).
source: Sox21a, a group B Sox protein, is preferentially expressed in the committed progenitor named enteroblast (EB) to promote enterocyte differentiation.
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1

claim: Sox21a promotes enterocyte differentiation.
source: Sox21a, a group B Sox protein, is preferentially expressed in the committed progenitor named enteroblast (EB) to promote enterocyte differentiation.
evidence: Supported by loss-of-function and gain-of-function experiments shown in Figures 2 and 3

claim: In Sox21a mutants, EBs do not divide.
source: In Sox21a mutants, EBs do not divide, but cannot differentiate properly and have increased expression of mitogens, which then act as paracrine signals to promote intestinal stem cell (ISC) proliferation.
evidence: Supported by PH3 staining data showing mitotic cells are NRE-lacZ negative (Figure 4D-E)

claim: Sox21a mutant EBs cannot differentiate properly.
source: In Sox21a mutants, EBs do not divide, but cannot differentiate properly and have increased expression of mitogens, which then act as paracrine signals to promote intestinal stem cell (ISC) proliferation.
evidence: Supported by loss of Pdm1 expression in mutant clones (Figure 2J)

claim: Sox21a mutant EBs have increased expression of mitogens.
source: In Sox21a mutants, EBs do not divide, but cannot differentiate properly and have increased expression of mitogens, which then act as paracrine signals to promote intestinal stem cell (ISC) proliferation.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data and Spi-lacZ reporter expression (Figure 5A-C)

claim: Mitogens from Sox21a mutant EBs act as paracrine signals to promote ISC proliferation.
source: In Sox21a mutants, EBs do not divide, but cannot differentiate properly and have increased expression of mitogens, which then act as paracrine signals to promote intestinal stem cell (ISC) proliferation.
evidence: Supported by pERK staining showing enhanced signaling in ISCs adjacent to mutant EBs (Figure 5D-E)

claim: Loss of Sox21a leads to a feedback amplification loop between ISCs and EBs.
source: This leads to a feedback amplification loop for rapid production of differentiation-defective EBs and tumorigenesis.
evidence: Supported by the observation of increased ISC proliferation and EB accumulation in Sox21a mutants (Figures 2 and 4)

claim: The ISC-EB feedback amplification loop leads to tumorigenesis in Sox21a mutants.
source: This leads to a feedback amplification loop for rapid production of differentiation-defective EBs and tumorigenesis.
evidence: Supported by tumor formation data in Sox21a mutants (Figure 2C-D)

claim: Sox21a is temporally downregulated in EBs following intestinal damage.
source: Notably, in normal intestine following damage, Sox21a is temporally downregulated in EBs to allow the activation of the ISC-EB amplification loop for epithelial repair.
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data after DSS treatment (Figure 6B-C)

claim: Downregulation of Sox21a following damage allows activation of the ISC-EB amplification loop for epithelial repair.
source: Notably, in normal intestine following damage, Sox21a is temporally downregulated in EBs to allow the activation of the ISC-EB amplification loop for epithelial repair.
evidence: Supported by increased ISC proliferation during damage phase and suppression by Sox21a overexpression (Figure 6J)

claim: The Drosophila midgut epithelium is constantly replenished by adult intestinal stem cells (ISCs).
source: Like mammalian intestine, the Drosophila midgut epithelium is constantly replenished by adult intestinal stem cells (ISCs) (Micchelli and Perrimon, 2006; Ohlstein and Spradling, 2006), although at a relatively slower pace.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: Drosophila ISCs replenish the midgut epithelium at a relatively slower pace than mammalian ISCs.
source: Like mammalian intestine, the Drosophila midgut epithelium is constantly replenished by adult intestinal stem cells (ISCs) (Micchelli and Perrimon, 2006; Ohlstein and Spradling, 2006), although at a relatively slower pace.
evidence: Comparative statement based on established knowledge

claim: ISCs can be specifically marked by Delta (Dl).
source: The Drosophila ISC, which generates a relatively simple stem cell lineage, can be specifically marked by Delta (Dl), the Notch ligand.
evidence: Established marker used throughout the study

claim: Delta is the Notch ligand.
source: The Drosophila ISC, which generates a relatively simple stem cell lineage, can be specifically marked by Delta (Dl), the Notch ligand.
evidence: Established molecular identity

claim: After asymmetric division, an ISC produces a new ISC and an enteroblast (EB).
source: After each asymmetric division, an ISC will produce a new ISC and a committed progenitor cell named enteroblast (EB), which will further differentiate into either an enterocyte or an enteroendocrine cell, depending on the levels of Notch activation it received from ISCs (Ohlstein and Spradling, 2007).
evidence: Cited from prior literature

claim: EBs differentiate into either enterocytes or enteroendocrine cells depending on Notch activation levels.
source: After each asymmetric division, an ISC will produce a new ISC and a committed progenitor cell named enteroblast (EB), which will further differentiate into either an enterocyte or an enteroendocrine cell, depending on the levels of Notch activation it received from ISCs (Ohlstein and Spradling, 2007).
evidence: Cited from prior literature

claim: Enterocyte differentiation from EB requires high levels of Notch activation.
source: Enterocyte differentiation from EB requires high levels of Notch activation, and JAK/STAT signaling activity is required for both enterocyte and enteroendocrine cell differentiation from EB (Beebe et al., 2010; Jiang et al., 2009; Lin et al., 2010).
evidence: Cited from prior literature

claim: JAK/STAT signaling activity is required for both enterocyte and enteroendocrine cell differentiation from EB.
source: Enterocyte differentiation from EB requires high levels of Notch activation, and JAK/STAT signaling activity is required for both enterocyte and enteroendocrine cell differentiation from EB (Beebe et al., 2010; Jiang et al., 2009; Lin et al., 2010).
evidence: Cited from prior literature

claim: Enterocyte differentiation from EB requires downregulation of Escargot (Esg).
source: Enterocyte differentiation from EB requires downregulation of Escargot (Esg) and activation of Pdm1 (Korzelius et al., 2014; Loza-Coll et al., 2014), whereas enteroendocrine cell differentiation from EB requires release of the inhibition by the transcriptional repressor Tramtrack and activation of acheate-scute complex (AS-C) genes and Prospero (Pros), the enteroendocrine cell determination factor (Bardin et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2015; Zeng and Hou, 2015).
evidence: Cited from prior literature

claim: Enterocyte differentiation from EB requires activation of Pdm1.
source: Enterocyte differentiation from EB requires downregulation of Escargot (Esg) and activation of Pdm1 (Korzelius et al., 2014; Loza-Coll et al., 2014), whereas enteroendocrine cell differentiation from EB requires release of the inhibition by the transcriptional repressor Tramtrack and activation of acheate-scute complex (AS-C) genes and Prospero (Pros), the enteroendocrine cell determination factor (Bardin et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2015; Zeng and Hou, 2015).
evidence: Cited from prior literature

claim: Sox21a RNA expression was detected only in ISCs and EBs.
source: From cell-type specific gene expression analysis of Drosophila midgut cells (Dutta et al., 2015 and unpublished data), we noticed a Sox family gene, Sox21a, whose RNA expression was detected only in ISCs and EBs.
evidence: Based on gene expression analysis

claim: Sox21a is mainly expressed in midgut, but not other organs in larva and adult Drosophila.
source: Interestingly, Sox21a seems to be mainly expressed in midgut, but not other organs in larva and adult Drosophila (Chintapalli et al., 2007).
evidence: Cited from prior literature

claim: Sox21a was largely undetectable in the midgut of newly eclosed and young flies of two to three days old.
source: Immunostaining of the wild type midgut with this antisera revealed that Sox21a was largely undetectable in the midgut of newly eclosed and young flies of two to three days old (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data in Figure 1A

claim: Sox21a expression begins to appear with age and at 4-5 days old, weak Sox21a expression appeared specifically in Dl+ ISCs and Notch-activated EBs.
source: Its expression began to appear with age and at 4–5 days old, weak Sox21a expression appeared specifically in Dl+ ISCs and Notch-activated EBs that can be marked by a Notch activation reporter, Su(H)Gbe>GFP (NRE>GFP) (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data in Figure 1B

claim: At 7 days old, Sox21a expression could be detected in early ECs.
source: At 7 days old, its expression could also be detected in early ECs, which display increased cell ploidy (Figure 1C–D).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data in Figure 1C-D

claim: In each ISC-EB pair, the level of Sox21a expression was usually higher in EB than in ISC.
source: In each ISC-EB pair, the level of Sox21a expression was usually higher in EB than in ISC (Figure 1C,F).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining and quantification in Figure 1C and 1F

claim: In each progenitor cell nest, the early EC usually displayed a higher Sox21a expression level than the EB or the ISC.
source: In each progenitor cell nest where the early EC still retained NRE>GFP expression, the early EC usually displayed a higher Sox21a expression level than the EB or the ISC in the same ISC-EB-early-EC cell nest (Figure 1D,F), suggesting that Sox21a is up-regulated in differentiating EBs.
evidence: Supported by immunostaining and quantification in Figure 1D and 1F

claim: Sox21a is up-regulated in differentiating EBs.
source: In each progenitor cell nest where the early EC still retained NRE>GFP expression, the early EC usually displayed a higher Sox21a expression level than the EB or the ISC in the same ISC-EB-early-EC cell nest (Figure 1D,F), suggesting that Sox21a is up-regulated in differentiating EBs.
evidence: Inferred from the progressive increase in Sox21a expression from ISC to EB to early EC

claim: EB differentiation requires mesenchymal-epithelial transition through downregulation of Esg.
source: Previous studies suggest that EB differentiation requires mesenchymal-epithelial transition through downregulation of Esg (Antonello et al., 2015; Korzelius et al., 2014).
evidence: Cited from prior literature

claim: In fixed midgut where Sox21a was not expressed, EBs commonly displayed triangle-shaped morphology.
source: Interestingly, in fixed midgut where Sox21a was not expressed, EBs commonly displayed triangle-shaped morphology (Figure 1A).
evidence: Observed in immunostaining data in Figure 1A

claim: Triangle-shaped EBs are probably dormant EBs that remain in the undifferentiated state.
source: We propose that these EBs are probably the dormant EBs that remain in the undifferentiated state (Figure 1H).
evidence: Proposed interpretation based on morphological observations

claim: In EBs where Sox21a began to be expressed, EBs displayed oval-shaped morphology.
source: By contrast, in EBs where Sox21a began to be expressed, EBs instead displayed oval-shaped morphology (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: Observed in immunostaining data in Figure 1C-D

claim: Oval-shaped EBs are likely activated EBs that are undergoing mesenchymal-epithelial transition.
source: These EBs are likely the activated EBs that are undergoing mesenchymal-epithelial transition (Figure 1H).
evidence: Proposed interpretation based on morphological observations and Sox21a expression

claim: Two Sox21a deletion alleles (JC1 and JC2) carry approximately 2.15 kb and 2.65 kb DNA fragment deletions, respectively.
source: we generated two gene deletion lines using the CRISPR/Cas9 system, and named these two alleles as Sox21a [JC1] and Sox21a [JC2], which carries approximately 2.15 kb and 2.65 kb DNA fragment deletion, respectively, in the gene locus (Figure 2A).
evidence: Described in methods and shown in Figure 2A

claim: Sox21a JC1 and JC2 alleles can be regarded as null alleles for Sox21a.
source: Because the coding region of Sox21a is almost entirely deleted in both alleles, they can be regarded as null alleles for Sox21a.
evidence: Based on the extent of deletion covering the coding region

claim: Sox21a homozygous mutant flies are viable and fertile.
source: Consistent with the midgut-restricted expression during development, Sox21a homozygous mutant flies are viable and fertile.
evidence: Observed phenotype of mutant flies

claim: The general gut morphology and cellular makeup of the monolayer midgut epithelium was largely normal in newly eclosed Sox21a mutants.
source: Staining midgut of newly eclosed mutants showed that the general gut morphology and the cellular makeup of the monolayer midgut epithelium was largely normal, although the epithelial cells appeared to be more sparsely distributed in the epithelium compared to the wild type intestinal epithelium (Figure 2B).
evidence: Observed in immunostaining data in Figure 2B

claim: Epithelial cells in newly eclosed Sox21a mutants appeared to be more sparsely distributed than in wild type.
source: Staining midgut of newly eclosed mutants showed that the general gut morphology and the cellular makeup of the monolayer midgut epithelium was largely normal, although the epithelial cells appeared to be more sparsely distributed in the epithelium compared to the wild type intestinal epithelium (Figure 2B).
evidence: Observed in immunostaining data in Figure 2B

claim: Sox21a could have a role in regulating the proliferation of midgut progenitor cells during development.
source: This indicates that Sox21a could have a role in regulating the proliferation of midgut progenitor cells during development.
evidence: Inferred from the sparse distribution of cells in newly eclosed mutants

claim: When Sox21a mutant flies got older, multilayered cell clusters composed of 50 or more cells were frequently observed in both anterior and posterior midgut.
source: Strikingly, when the mutant flies got older, multilayered cell clusters composed of 50 or more cells (termed tumors hereafter) were frequently observed in both anterior and posterior midgut, and tumor incidence steadily increased with age (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: Observed in immunostaining and quantified in Figure 2C-D

claim: Tumor incidence in Sox21a mutants steadily increased with age.
source: Strikingly, when the mutant flies got older, multilayered cell clusters composed of 50 or more cells (termed tumors hereafter) were frequently observed in both anterior and posterior midgut, and tumor incidence steadily increased with age (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: Quantified in Figure 2D

claim: At day 6 after eclosion, approximately 49.1% and 57.9% of JC1 and JC2 homozygous female flies had at least one tumor in the midgut, respectively.
source: At day 6 after eclosion, approximately 49.1% and 57.9% of [JC1] and [JC2] homozygous female flies had at least one tumor in the midgut, respectively, and at day 11, approximately 77.3% and 94.1% of [JC1] and [JC2] flies had gut tumors, respectively (Figure 2D).
evidence: Quantified in Figure 2D

claim: At day 11, approximately 77.3% and 94.1% of JC1 and JC2 flies had gut tumors, respectively.
source: At day 6 after eclosion, approximately 49.1% and 57.9% of [JC1] and [JC2] homozygous female flies had at least one tumor in the midgut, respectively, and at day 11, approximately 77.3% and 94.1% of [JC1] and [JC2] flies had gut tumors, respectively (Figure 2D).
evidence: Quantified in Figure 2D

claim: Tumor size grew with time in Sox21a mutants.
source: Tumor size also grew with time, and in aged mutants, the tumor masses often filled up the entire lumen space, suggesting that tumors grow rapidly once it is initiated.
evidence: Observed in aged mutant flies

claim: Tumors grow rapidly once initiated in Sox21a mutants.
source: Tumor size also grew with time, and in aged mutants, the tumor masses often filled up the entire lumen space, suggesting that tumors grow rapidly once it is initiated.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that tumor masses filled the entire lumen space

claim: NRE-lacZ+ EBs are more sparsely distributed in the epithelium of the mutant intestine than of the wild type intestine at day 2 after eclosion.
source: Like all other cells, the Su(H)Gbe-lacZ (NRE-lacZ)+ EBs are more sparsely distributed in the epithelium of the mutant intestine than of the wild type intestine at day 2 after eclosion (Figure 2E,F).
evidence: Observed in immunostaining data in Figure 2E-F

claim: NRE-lacZ+ cells rapidly accumulated in the epithelium of the mutant intestine at day 7.
source: However, the NRE-lacZ+ cells rapidly accumulated in the epithelium of the mutant intestine at day 7 (Figure 2G,G').
evidence: Observed in immunostaining data in Figure 2G-G'

claim: Sox21a mutants postnatally develop intestinal tumors.
source: Thus, Sox21a mutants postnatally develop intestinal tumors.
evidence: Inferred from the temporal progression of tumor development

claim: ISCs and EBs were intermingled with each other in EB-accumulated regions of Sox21a mutants.
source: Co-staining Dl with NRE-lacZ revealed that ISCs and EBs were intermingled with each other in EB-accumulated regions (Figure 2G,G').
evidence: Observed in immunostaining data in Figure 2G-G'

claim: The tumors in Sox21a mutant intestine are mainly composed of ISCs and EBs.
source: Those observations suggest that the tumors in Sox21a mutant intestine are mainly composed of ISCs and EBs, and indicate that Sox21a might be required for EB differentiation.
evidence: Inferred from the cell type markers in tumor regions

claim: Sox21a might be required for EB differentiation.
source: Those observations suggest that the tumors in Sox21a mutant intestine are mainly composed of ISCs and EBs, and indicate that Sox21a might be required for EB differentiation.
evidence: Inferred from the accumulation of undifferentiated EBs in mutants

claim: Sox21a homozygous mutant clones cell-autonomously gave rise to intestinal tumors mainly composed of NRE-lacZ+ cells intermingled with Dl+ cells.
source: As expected, the mutant clones cell-autonomously gave rise to intestinal tumors which was mainly composed of NRE-lacZ+ cells intermingled with Dl+ cells (Figure 2H,H').
evidence: Observed in MARCM clone analysis in Figure 2H-H'

claim: There was mild increase of Dl+ cells that were scatteredly distributed within Sox21a mutant clones.
source: There was also mild increase of Dl+ cells that were scatteredly distributed within the mutant clones (Figure 2I,I').
evidence: Observed in immunostaining data in Figure 2I-I'

claim: Pros+ cells could rarely but occasionally be found in Sox21a mutant clones.
source: Rarely but occasionally Pros+ cells could be found in the mutant clones (Figure 2I and data not shown), indicating that Sox21a is not absolutely required for enteroendocrine cell differentiation.
evidence: Observed in immunostaining data in Figure 2I

claim: Sox21a is not absolutely required for enteroendocrine cell differentiation.
source: Rarely but occasionally Pros+ cells could be found in the mutant clones (Figure 2I and data not shown), indicating that Sox21a is not absolutely required for enteroendocrine cell differentiation.
evidence: Inferred from the presence of some Pros+ cells in mutant clones

claim: Polyploid cells were found in Sox21a mutant clones but their size was relatively smaller than ECs.
source: Polyploid cells were also found in the clones but their size was relatively smaller than ECs (Figure 2I–J).
evidence: Observed in immunostaining data in Figure 2I-J

claim: Pdm1 failed to be expressed in Sox21a mutant cells in a cell-autonomous manner.
source: Interestingly, Pdm1, an enterocyte marker (Lee et al., 2009), failed to be expressed in Sox21a mutant cells in a cell-autonomous manner (Figure 2I,I').
evidence: Observed in immunostaining data in Figure 2J-J'

claim: Sox21a is cell-autonomously required for EB differentiation into enterocyte.
source: These observations suggest that Sox21a is cell-autonomously required for EB differentiation into enterocyte.
evidence: Inferred from the cell-autonomous loss of Pdm1 expression in mutant clones

claim: Sox21a is required for the expression of Pdm1.
source: The above results demonstrate that Sox21a is required for the expression of Pdm1.
evidence: Demonstrated by loss of Pdm1 in Sox21a mutants

claim: Pdm1 expression is sufficient to induce differentiation of progenitor cell into enterocyte.
source: Because Pdm1 expression is sufficient to induce differentiation of progenitor cell into enterocyte (Korzelius et al., 2014), Sox21a may function to promote enterocyte differentiation by inducing Pdm1 expression.
evidence: Cited from prior literature

claim: Sox21a may function to promote enterocyte differentiation by inducing Pdm1 expression.
source: Because Pdm1 expression is sufficient to induce differentiation of progenitor cell into enterocyte (Korzelius et al., 2014), Sox21a may function to promote enterocyte differentiation by inducing Pdm1 expression.
evidence: Inferred from the requirement of Sox21a for Pdm1 expression and the sufficiency of Pdm1 for differentiation

claim: Virtually all Esg>GFP+ cells were negative for Pdm1 expression under normal conditions.
source: Under normal conditions, virtually all Esg>GFP+ cells were negative for Pdm1 expression (Figure 3A,A').
evidence: Observed in immunostaining data in Figure 3A-A'

claim: When Sox21a was forcibly expressed for 5 days, approximately 34.2 ± 1.6% of Esg>GFP+ cells became positive for Pdm1 expression.
source: However, when Sox21a was forcibly expressed for 5 days, approximately 34.2 ± 1.6% of Esg>GFP+ cells became positive for Pdm1 expression (Figure 3B,B',E).
evidence: Quantified in Figure 3E from immunostaining data

claim: The Pdm1+ cells induced by Sox21a overexpression were always one of the GFP+ ISC-EB pairs.
source: The Pdm1+ cells were always one of the GFP+ ISC-EB pairs, indicating that expression of Sox21a could not induce Pdm1 expression in ISCs, but EBs (Figure 3B,B').
evidence: Observed in immunostaining data in Figure 3B-B'

claim: Expression of Sox21a could not induce Pdm1 expression in ISCs, but in EBs.
source: The Pdm1+ cells were always one of the GFP+ ISC-EB pairs, indicating that expression of Sox21a could not induce Pdm1 expression in ISCs, but EBs (Figure 3B,B').
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Pdm1+ cells were always in the EB position of ISC-EB pairs

claim: Transient induction of Sox21 expression for 5 days induced approximately 72.3 ± 3.8% of NRE>GFP+ cells to turn on Pdm1 expression.
source: Indeed, transient induction of Sox21 expression for 5 days induced approximately 72.3 ± 3.8% of NRE>GFP+ cells to turn on Pdm1 expression (Figure 3D,D',E), and these cells began to show polyploidy, indicating that they are in the process of enterocyte differentiation (Figure 3D,D').
evidence: Quantified in Figure 3E from immunostaining data

claim: Cells induced to express Pdm1 by Sox21a overexpression in EBs began to show polyploidy.
source: Indeed, transient induction of Sox21 expression for 5 days induced approximately 72.3 ± 3.8% of NRE>GFP+ cells to turn on Pdm1 expression (Figure 3D,D',E), and these cells began to show polyploidy, indicating that they are in the process of enterocyte differentiation (Figure 3D,D').
evidence: Observed in immunostaining data in Figure 3D-D'

claim: Cells showing polyploidy after Sox21a overexpression are in the process of enterocyte differentiation.
source: Indeed, transient induction of Sox21 expression for 5 days induced approximately 72.3 ± 3.8% of NRE>GFP+ cells to turn on Pdm1 expression (Figure 3D,D',E), and these cells began to show polyploidy, indicating that they are in the process of enterocyte differentiation (Figure 3D,D').
evidence: Inferred from the known association between polyploidy and enterocyte differentiation

claim: ISC-containing clones with constitutive Sox21a overexpression grew normally in size.
source: The ISC-containing clones grew normally in size and were able to produce both polyploidy enterocytes and Pros+ enteroendocrine cells (Figure 3F), suggesting that forced Sox21a expression does not inhibit ISC activity and does not block enteroendocrine cell differentiation.
evidence: Observed in MARCM clone analysis in Figure 3F

claim: ISC-containing clones with constitutive Sox21a overexpression were able to produce both polyploidy enterocytes and Pros+ enteroendocrine cells.
source: The ISC-containing clones grew normally in size and were able to produce both polyploidy enterocytes and Pros+ enteroendocrine cells (Figure 3F), suggesting that forced Sox21a expression does not inhibit ISC activity and does not block enteroendocrine cell differentiation.
evidence: Observed in MARCM clone analysis in Figure 3F

claim: Forced Sox21a expression does not inhibit ISC activity.
source: The ISC-containing clones grew normally in size and were able to produce both polyploidy enterocytes and Pros+ enteroendocrine cells (Figure 3F), suggesting that forced Sox21a expression does not inhibit ISC activity and does not block enteroendocrine cell differentiation.
evidence: Inferred from normal clone growth and cell production

claim: Forced Sox21a expression does not block enteroendocrine cell differentiation.
source: The ISC-containing clones grew normally in size and were able to produce both polyploidy enterocytes and Pros+ enteroendocrine cells (Figure 3F), suggesting that forced Sox21a expression does not inhibit ISC activity and does not block enteroendocrine cell differentiation.
evidence: Inferred from the presence of Pros+ cells in Sox21a overexpression clones

claim: Sox21a overexpression is not sufficient to induce differentiation of ISCs.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that Sox21a overexpression is not sufficient to induce differentiation of ISCs, but is able to induce precocious differentiation of EBs by inducing Pdm1 expression.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Pdm1 induction occurs only in EBs, not ISCs

claim: Sox21a overexpression is able to induce precocious differentiation of EBs by inducing Pdm1 expression.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that Sox21a overexpression is not sufficient to induce differentiation of ISCs, but is able to induce precocious differentiation of EBs by inducing Pdm1 expression.
evidence: Supported by the induction of Pdm1 and polyploidy in EBs upon Sox21a overexpression

claim: The tumor cells in Sox21a mutants had strikingly high ability to incorporate BrdU.
source: BrdU incorporation assay revealed that the tumor cells had strikingly high ability to incorporate BrdU (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: Observed in BrdU incorporation assay in Figure 4A-B

claim: The mutant intestine had exponentially increased number of mitotic cells with age.
source: As expected, the mutant intestine had exponentially increased number of mitotic cells with age (Figure 4C).
evidence: Quantified in Figure 4C

claim: Significantly increased number of mitotic cells was found in the tumors compared to non-tumor areas.
source: In addition, significantly increased number of mitotic cells was found in the tumors compared to non-tumor areas (not shown).
evidence: Stated as observed data

claim: The increased mitotic activity drives tumor growth in Sox21a mutants.
source: These observations indicate that the increased mitotic activity drives tumor growth.
evidence: Inferred from the correlation between mitotic activity and tumor growth

claim: Virtually all mitotic cells in Sox21a mutant tumors were NRE-lacZ- (353 out of 354).
source: Surprisingly, virtually all mitotic cells in the tumor were NRE-lacZ- (353 out of 354) (Figure 4D–E).
evidence: Quantified from immunostaining data in Figure 4D-E

claim: The proliferative cells that drive tumor growth in Sox21a mutants are not EBs but ISCs.
source: Thus, the proliferative cells that drive tumor growth are not EBs but ISCs.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that mitotic cells are NRE-lacZ negative (not EBs)

claim: Specifically knocking down Sox21a by RNAi in EBs was sufficient to induce rapid accumulation of EB-like cells in the intestinal epithelium.
source: However, Specifically knocking down Sox21a by RNAi (HMJ21395 or JF02191) in EBs using Su(H)Gbe-Gal4,UAS-GFP; Tub-Gal80ts (referred to as NRE-Gal4ts) was sufficient to induce rapid accumulation of EB-like cells in the intestinal epithelium (Figure 4F,G), a phenotype largely similar to that observed in Sox21a mutant intestine.
evidence: Observed in RNAi knockdown experiments in Figure 4F-G

claim: Loss of Sox21a in EB is sufficient to induce tumor development.
source: Therefore, loss of Sox21a in EB is sufficient to induce tumor development, indicating that Sox21a mutant EBs are tumor-initiating cells, although they are non-mitotic cells.
evidence: Inferred from the sufficiency of EB-specific Sox21a knockdown to induce tumors

claim: Sox21a mutant EBs are tumor-initiating cells, although they are non-mitotic cells.
source: Therefore, loss of Sox21a in EB is sufficient to induce tumor development, indicating that Sox21a mutant EBs are tumor-initiating cells, although they are non-mitotic cells.
evidence: Inferred from the sufficiency of EB-specific Sox21a loss to induce tumors and the observation that EBs are non-mitotic

claim: EB-specific expression of Sox21a largely suppressed intestinal tumor formation in Sox21a mutants.
source: Indeed, EB-specific expression of Sox21a largely suppressed intestinal tumor formation in both anterior and posterior midgut of Sox21a mutants (Figure 4H).
evidence: Quantified in Figure 4H

claim: ISC-specific expression of Sox21a failed to suppress intestinal tumor formation in Sox21a mutants.
source: By contrast, ISC-specific expression of Sox21a failed to suppress intestinal tumor formation in Sox21a mutants (Figure 4H).
evidence: Quantified in Figure 4H

claim: EB is the tumor-initiating cell that is necessary and sufficient for intestinal tumor development in Sox21a mutant intestine.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that EB is the tumor-initiating cell that is necessary and sufficient for intestinal tumor development in Sox21a mutant intestine.
evidence: Inferred from the sufficiency of EB-specific Sox21a loss to induce tumors and the necessity of EB-specific Sox21a expression to suppress tumors

claim: Sox21a mutant EBs must non-cell autonomously induce ISC proliferation to promote tumor formation.
source: Because Sox21a mutant EBs are non-mitotic yet are responsible for tumor initiation, the mutant EBs must non-cell autonomously induce ISC proliferation to promote tumor formation.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that EBs are non-mitotic but ISCs are proliferative in tumors

claim: Multiple secreted growth factors were found to be up-regulated by two fold or more in Sox21a-depleted cells, including Spitz (Spi), Upd3, Pvf2 and Pvf1.
source: Multiple secreted growth factors were found to be up-regulated by two fold or more in Sox21a-depleted cells, including Spitz (Spi), a ligand for EGFR/Ras/MAPK signaling, Upd3, a ligand for JAK/STAT signaling, and Pvf2 and Pvf1, which also induces Ras/MAPK signaling via PVR (Figure 5A).
evidence: Identified from RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5A

claim: Spitz (Spi) is a ligand for EGFR/Ras/MAPK signaling.
source: Multiple secreted growth factors were found to be up-regulated by two fold or more in Sox21a-depleted cells, including Spitz (Spi), a ligand for EGFR/Ras/MAPK signaling, Upd3, a ligand for JAK/STAT signaling, and Pvf2 and Pvf1, which also induces Ras/MAPK signaling via PVR (Figure 5A).
evidence: Established molecular identity

claim: Upd3 is a ligand for JAK/STAT signaling.
source: Multiple secreted growth factors were found to be up-regulated by two fold or more in Sox21a-depleted cells, including Spitz (Spi), a ligand for EGFR/Ras/MAPK signaling, Upd3, a ligand for JAK/STAT signaling, and Pvf2 and Pvf1, which also induces Ras/MAPK signaling via PVR (Figure 5A).
evidence: Established molecular identity

claim: Pvf2 and Pvf1 induce Ras/MAPK signaling via PVR.
source: Multiple secreted growth factors were found to be up-regulated by two fold or more in Sox21a-depleted cells, including Spitz (Spi), a ligand for EGFR/Ras/MAPK signaling, Upd3, a ligand for JAK/STAT signaling, and Pvf2 and Pvf1, which also induces Ras/MAPK signaling via PVR (Figure 5A).
evidence: Established molecular pathway

claim: Spi, Upd3, Pvf2 and Pvf1 all function as positive regulators of ISC proliferation during normal homeostasis and/or in response to injury or infection.
